title: NEB Class 11 Biology — Ecology — 2024
subject: biology
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: Define ecosystem. Describe the structure of an ecosystem with a diagram description.
questions.solution:
**Ecosystem:** organisms plus their physical environment functioning as one unit.

**Abiotic:** light, temperature, water, soil, minerals. **Biotic:** producers (plants) → primary consumers (herbivores) → secondary/tertiary consumers (carnivores) → decomposers (bacteria, fungi) recycling nutrients back to soil.

(Draw nested boxes: environment enclosing trophic levels in feeding order, decomposers arrowing back to producers.)
questions.knowledgeNote: Energy flows one way (10% rule); nutrients cycle — the two traffic laws of every ecosystem diagram.

questions.question: What is ecological succession? Explain with the example of xerosere.
questions.solution:
**Succession** is the ordered replacement of communities over time toward a stable climax.

**Xerosere** (bare rock → forest): lichens (pioneers, weather rock) → mosses → herbs → shrubs → forest (climax). Each stage builds soil and shade for the next.
questions.knowledgeNote: Xerosere (dry rock) vs hydrosere (open water): opposite starts, both ending in forest climax.

questions.question: Distinguish between a food chain and a food web. What is the ten percent law?
questions.solution:
**Food chain:** a single feeding line (grass → deer → tiger). **Food web:** the interlinked mesh of all chains — realistic, stable, with alternate routes if one prey fails.

**Ten percent law (Lindeman):** only ~10% of energy transfers per trophic level; the rest is lost as heat/respiration — which is why food chains rarely exceed 4–5 levels.
questions.knowledgeNote: Short chains feed more people per hectare — the energetics behind vegetarian efficiency arguments.

questions.question: What are ecological pyramids? Explain why the pyramid of energy is always upright.
questions.solution:
Graphic trophic structure as pyramids of **number**, **biomass**, or **energy**.

Number/biomass pyramids can invert (one tree feeding many birds; tiny phytoplankton feeding bulky zooplankton). But **energy** pyramids are always upright — each level holds only ~10% of the one below, so higher levels can never out-energy their base.
questions.knowledgeNote: Upright-energy is thermodynamically forced; inverted-number/biomass are sampling artefacts of size differences.

questions.question: Describe any three types of population interaction with one example of each.
questions.solution: **Competition** (−/−): two species lose together — weeds vs paddy. **Predation** (+/−): tiger eats deer. **Mutualism** (+/+): lichen (fungus + alga) or legume–Rhizobium. (Also: parasitism +/−, commensalism +/0, amensalism −/0.)
questions.knowledgeNote: The +/− sign code compresses every interaction into two symbols — learn it once, answer any of them.

questions.question: What is eutrophication? Explain its causes and effects on aquatic life.
questions.solution:
**Eutrophication** is nutrient enrichment (nitrates, phosphates from fertilisers/sewage) triggering algal blooms.

Blooms block light, then die and decompose — decomposition devours dissolved oxygen (BOD spike) → fish suffocate, biodiversity collapses, lakes turn to dead marshes.
questions.knowledgeNote: Phewa Lake's water-hyacinth choking is Nepal's textbook eutrophication case.
